report:
**Conclusion: No.** Reliable randomized-trial evidence does not show that ivermectin lowers the risk of death from COVID-19.

Why the earlier “yes” impression arose: early small studies and meta-analyses reported striking mortality benefits, but many were imprecise, at high risk of bias, or later subject to serious quality concerns. Results from small, flawed trials can disproportionately distort a meta-analysis.

Better evidence came from larger, placebo-controlled randomized trials. In the TOGETHER trial of high-risk symptomatic outpatients, ivermectin did **not** reduce COVID-19 progression requiring hospital admission or prolonged emergency observation versus placebo. The paper also notes that a previously reported ivermectin trial had been withdrawn amid suspected malfeasance, illustrating why trial quality matters.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869

ACTIV-6, a large U.S. randomized placebo-controlled trial, likewise tested ivermectin in outpatients; its higher-dose follow-up was designed because the earlier dose had not demonstrated meaningful clinical benefit.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2797483  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2801827

The 2022 Cochrane systematic review assessed ivermectin for COVID-19 treatment and prevention, incorporating the evolving evidence base rather than relying on early positive reports.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD015017.pub3/abstract

Ivermectin remains a useful prescription antiparasitic for its approved indications, but it is not FDA-authorized or approved to prevent or treat COVID-19; inappropriate use, especially veterinary products or excessive doses, can cause serious harm.  
https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/ivermectin-and-covid-19
